gaps.note: Arc. Three of four deltas cite docs.arc.io and the only cleared item for this lens is about Multicall3From. No unit read where the client resets transient storage between transactions or how the blocklist check before execution is run. The endpoint reports client version arc/v1 and refuses eth_simulateV1 and eth_callMany, so the critic's two transaction simulation could not run here.

Arc. The token contract at 0x3600 is the only caller of Native Coin Authority, which can move any native balance, and its implementation source was not read. The profile rests on documentation and two repository files.

Avalanche. The profile and the cleared items rest on docs.avax.network and one RPC read. The source of the new execution engine was not read for the transient storage reset, for atomic transactions or for end of block operations. The public endpoint (avalanchego 1.15.3) has no eth_simulateV1.

Avalanche. The precompile list was taken from documentation. No call from the PoolManager address to the precompile addresses with transfer, balanceOf, the hook selectors or empty calldata is recorded, although that sweep was the assigned angle.

BNB Smart Chain and Polygon. The system contract ranges (0x1000 to 0x1008, 0x2000 to 0x2006 and 0x3000 on BNB Smart Chain, 0x1000 and 0x1001 on Polygon, all of which hold code today) have no recorded sweep with the call shapes P1, P2, P3 and P5. Only 0x1010 on Polygon was tested.

OP Stack chains with ETH gas. Predeploys were tested as hook addresses and two of them as currencies (WETH and LegacyERC20ETH). No sweep of 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff with transfer, balanceOf and empty calldata from the PoolManager is recorded, and the profiles of Zora, Ink, Soneium and World Chain repeat the generic OP Stack text.

World Chain. The endpoint reports world-chain v2.8.2, a separate node build. The profile cites OP Stack documents and one probe. The transaction gas cap is unconfirmed against a 280,000,000 block gas limit, and the RPC refuses simulation methods.

Elysium. The profile rests on project documentation and assumes stock Nitro. Elysium settles to HyperEVM, so its forced inclusion path, its bridge escrow and its data availability depend on a parent chain with 3,000,000 gas blocks and HyperCore system transactions. No unit looked at that dependency.

Robinhood Chain. The rule set of the transaction filter is unknown and two of six deltas cite dashboards (ethbeat.org, dune.com). The verifier counted 6,234 add events and the profile quotes about 1,351 filtered hashes. What an entry identifies was not established.

HyperEVM. The clearance of assumption A1 uses the public replay client. The verdict on the system transaction finding says that this client has no branch for the AQAv2 senders, so the clearance does not cover those transactions. One delta cites a Telegram post.

MegaETH. Eight of nine deltas cite docs.megaeth.com. The mega-evm source was not read for the gas forwarding rule, the resource budgets or the volatile data rule. The low finding on volatile data has evidence marked inferred.

X Layer. The caller address of the gasless whitelist system call is unconfirmed, the hardfork activated with xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 is unidentified, and no source was read for the transient storage reset in the X Layer fork of the client.
Arbitrum One. Four deltas. The tokens held by the PoolManager were not listed or classified, and the issuer control finding that five other units raised was not checked here.

Polygon and Avalanche. A blocklist entry by the USDC issuer is recorded as a cleared item with the remark that it would freeze every USDC pool. Five other units report the same hazard as a high finding. The state should hold it as one finding that lists these chains.
Zora, Ink and Soneium. The profiles name the main stablecoins only. Zora has no delta of high relevance in any lens, which suggests the assets of its pools were not read from chain.

Unichain. The PoolManager is a genesis predeploy of 24,050 bytes against 24,009 elsewhere, and every Unichain clearance assumes it behaves like src/. Three units ask for a bytecode comparison. The owner has forbidden comparing this code with other copies, so this cell stays open until the owner names an accepted method. The next cycle should not run a comparison on its own.

Celo. The unit did not test the fee currency adapters as pool currencies. Critic check on forno.celo.org at block 0x4f97135 with from set to the PoolManager: the four adapters in FeeCurrencyDirectory (0x0e2a3e05bc9a16f5292a6170456a710cb89c6f72, 0x2f25deb3848c207fc8e0c34035b3ba7fc157602b, 0x0357ee22278c922e1d36cfe6b899269b161880c4, 0x857bf24e29da0773687e804a743c2e421a394c16) answer balanceOf(PoolManager) with the balance of the adapted token scaled to 18 decimals and revert on transfer(address,uint256). They behave like LegacyERC20ETH: sync succeeds, a credit under the adapter id needs a real payment of the adapted token, and take reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). This can be recorded as cleared.

Critic check of assumption A1 on 2026-11-22, read only. An eth_call creation probe on all 21 RPC endpoints showed that a TSTORE is rolled back when its frame reverts, that it is rolled back when an outer frame reverts after the inner frame succeeded, that TSTORE fails under STATICCALL, and that a committed value is visible to later calls in the same transaction. A two transaction simulation with a state override contract returned zero for TLOAD in the second transaction on 13 endpoints through eth_simulateV1 (chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 130, 7777777, 57073, 1868, 42161, 4663, 99901, 137, 56, 4217) and on MegaETH through eth_callMany. The seven chains listed here refuse both methods. These results describe the RPC node of each network and its simulation path. They do not replace a reading of the block production code.

titles: Thirteen Wormhole guardians can act as PoolManager owner on BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche
Thirteen Wormhole guardians can act as PoolManager owner on Monad and MegaETH
The owner on HyperEVM is a Wormhole message receiver, so a guardian quorum can exercise the owner role
PoolManager ownership on Tempo and Arc is exercised through Wormhole guardian signatures
duplicates.note: One hazard on seven chains (56, 43114, 143, 4326, 999, 4217, 5042). The arbitrum-family unit recorded the same owner path on Elysium (99901) as a cleared item. Merge into one finding that lists all eight chains, and move the Elysium item from cleared to that finding.

titles: PoolManager ownership rests on an upgradeable messenger predeploy on five chains and on the portal alias on two, and a takeover reaches protocol fees only
PoolManager ownership on Celo and X Layer rests on the upgradeable L2CrossDomainMessenger, and on X Layer a 2 of 3 Safe of EOAs can upgrade it
duplicates.note: Same hazard on nine OP Stack chains. Both verdicts raised it to medium, while the Wormhole owner path and the Polygon state sync owner path stayed low with the same reach (the protocol fee of at most 0.1 percent per direction and accrued fees). The severity scale should be applied the same way to all owner path findings.

titles: One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
Blacklist and freeze roles on the pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them, because one address holds all balances
Blacklist and freeze roles on pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them on Monad and MegaETH
USDC and USDT0 issuers can block the PoolManager address, which stops every pool in that currency, and USDT0's owner can burn the blocked balance
Circle's blocklist covers native USDC on Arc, so one entry for the PoolManager freezes native and ERC-20 USDC pools together
duplicates.note: One hazard reported by five units for eleven chains (1, 10, 8453, 130, 480, 57073, 1868, 143, 4326, 999, 5042). The Arc case adds the native face and should stay a separate variant. The established-l1 unit lists the same hazard for Polygon and Avalanche as cleared, which contradicts the high rating given elsewhere.

titles: B20 precompile tokens on Base give the issuer seize, pause and policy control over the PoolManager balance, and their rules change at hard forks
TIP-20 issuer roles can burn, freeze or pause the PoolManager balance of a Tempo stablecoin
Scheduled Jenner fork adds protocol-native tokens whose issuer can seize, pause or block the PoolManager balance
Robinhood Stock Tokens and USDG let the issuer block, pause, burn or upgrade the tokens held by the PoolManager
duplicates.note: Same class on four chains: a token standard run by the chain or by one issuer with freeze and seize roles. Keep one finding per chain and link them. The Base and Tempo verdicts both name the account 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246 as policy admin for OUSD (policy 122 on Base, policy 2 on Tempo), and each verifier wrote a high lead about it. One answer serves both.

titles: A pool's hook can block or reprice every liquidity removal in that pool, and core has no path that skips the hook
EIP-7702 lets the code behind a hook address be replaced or removed after a pool is created
A Stylus program used as a hook or token stops answering calls on expiry or a Stylus version change, and activation is blocked
duplicates.note: The second and third are network variants of the first. The verifier of the accounting unit already said so for EIP-7702. Record them as variants of one finding with the general case on all 21 chains.

titles: sync runs while the manager is locked and fee collection ignores the lock, and the mainnet fee controller lets anyone trigger collection
Source disagrees with two interface comments and two test conditions, and none of the four changes who can move funds
duplicates.note: Both report that sync has no lock check and that collectProtocolFees never calls _isUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-60). Four network units also wrote leads on this, and the accounting unit and its verifier answered them with no fund effect. Close those leads together.

titles: Operator transaction filtering on Robinhood Chain can fail any exit from the PoolManager, including force-included ones
X Layer block builder can exclude PoolManager transactions through a rule driven risk control filter, which leaves L1 deposits as the exit
Soneium restricts listed contracts at its own RPC and sequencer, which leaves L1 forced inclusion as the exit for pools that touch a listed token or hook
MegaETH has one sequencer, so an exit from the PoolManager that it refuses to include depends on L1 forced inclusion with a 12 hour bound
duplicates.note: Same class: the operator can leave out transactions that touch the PoolManager. Three were rated low because forced inclusion remains. The Robinhood case is high because its filter also applies to forced transactions. Keep that distinction explicit when merging.

titles: Lead: what does lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol contain (asked by five units)
Lead: does the deployed PoolManager bytecode match a build of this repository (asked by three units)
duplicates.note: The Owned.sol leads are answered. Two verifiers read the file at the pinned commit: one storage variable, onlyOwner is a plain sender check, transferOwnership is the only other state changing function. The bytecode leads ask for a comparison that the owner has forbidden. They should wait for the owner's decision.

titles: Cleared: Whether anyone can use the protocol fee functions while protocolFeeController is the zero address
Cleared: whether anyone can call the PoolManager as the zero address, which is the protocol fee controller on both networks
Cleared: Whether a call can reach the PoolManager with msg.sender equal to address(0) on Celo and X Layer
duplicates.note: Contradiction. Two verifiers rejected the first two items because the Ecotone and Isthmus specifications define upgrade deposits sent from the zero address. The third item, for Celo and X Layer, was accepted although both are OP Stack chains with the controller at zero and did not consider upgrade deposits.

titles: Cleared: whether the SALT bucket multiplier lets an attacker raise storage gas until a liquidity removal or a take cannot be paid for
Verifier lead: a forced exit through the OptimismPortal can buy at most 20,000,000 gas per L1 block
duplicates.note: Contradiction on MegaETH. The researcher cleared the question with the 10,000,000,000 block gas limit. The verifier points out that the forced inclusion route is capped at 20,000,000 gas per L1 block, so a multiplier above about 1,000 on one zero to nonzero write would close that route. The item should stay open, not cleared.

titles: Cleared: tick spacing bounds, bitmap arithmetic, the liquidity cap per tick and overflow of in range liquidity
Severity scale: medium includes liquidity operations blocked without loss
duplicates.note: The accounting unit found that any account can fill the lowest or highest usable tick to the per tick cap for about 1.9e12 base units and so block every position that uses that tick, including full range positions, until it withdraws (src/libraries/Pool.sol:165-173). It filed this under cleared. Under the review rules this is griefing with no loss or freeze, which is consistent, but the scale would rate a blocked liquidity operation as medium. Decide once which rule applies and record the item accordingly.

leads.question: Where does the block production code of Arc (client arc/v1), Avalanche C-Chain (avalanchego 1.15.3), HyperEVM, X Layer (xlayer-reth v0.0.7) and World Chain (world-chain v2.8.2) discard transient storage between two transactions of one block, and does an RPC provider that offers eth_simulateV1 or eth_callMany for these chains return zero from TLOAD in a transaction that follows one that ran TSTORE on the same contract?
leads.why: sync needs no unlock and leaves the synced currency and reserves in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). If those two slots survived into a later transaction, any account could sync a token, wait for other users' deposits and settle the whole increase to itself (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). That would be a critical siphon. On 2026-11-22 the critic ran a read only two transaction simulation with a state override contract. The second transaction read zero on 13 endpoints through eth_simulateV1 (chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 130, 7777777, 57073, 1868, 42161, 4663, 99901, 137, 56, 4217) and on MegaETH through eth_callMany. The endpoints of these five chains and of Celo and Monad refuse both methods. Celo and Monad have a client source reading from this cycle. Arc has none, Avalanche rests on documentation, World Chain and X Layer rest on the OP Stack deposit text, and the HyperEVM clearance uses a replay client that does not model the AQAv2 system transactions. A simulation shows the RPC path only, so the place in the source is still needed.

leads.question: Does HyperCore require a signature or a CoreWriter action from the EVM address that becomes the sender of an AQAv2 system transaction, or can a treasury deployer name any EVM address, including a contract that cannot sign?
leads.why: This one fact settles the plausible finding on unsigned system transactions. If the address must consent, the PoolManager can never be a sender and the finding drops to info. If an address can be named, a system transaction could call transfer on a token with the PoolManager as msg.sender and lower its balance with no take and no delta (assumptions A2 and A8, src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The researcher and the verifier each asked part of this. The exchange API description of authorizeAqav2Role and one observed AQAv2 sender traced back to its authorisation answer it.

leads.question: On Robinhood Chain, what does each of the 6,234 entries added by the filterer account identify (a transaction hash, a sender, or any address touched during execution), is the list provider automated, and can an ordinary account cause an entry or a rule to match transactions that call the PoolManager 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951, for example by sending funds from a restricted address through a pool or by creating a pool whose hook or token touches a restricted address?
leads.why: The confirmed filtering finding assumes the operator has to act against the PoolManager. All pools, claims and protocol fees sit at one address (assumption A6), and the filter also fails force included transactions. If entries match addresses touched in execution and are added by an automated provider, a third party could make every exit through the shared address fail without holding any role, which would move the finding from the operator class to the unprivileged class.

leads.question: Without a compiler, does the source text satisfy every concrete expectation in the repository tests that no unit has replayed yet: test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol, Position.t.sol, TickBitmap.t.sol, SafeCast.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol, LPFeeLibrary.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol and BitMath.t.sol, test/CustomAccounting.t.sol, ERC6909Claims.t.sol, ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, PoolManager.clear.t.sol, PoolManagerInitialize.t.sol, NoDelegateCall.t.sol and DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, and the expectRevert cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol?
leads.why: The organisers say this build contains at least one path to frozen or siphoned funds, and no unit found one that an ordinary account can use. Both source readers worked from the text and replayed the vectors of SwapMath, SqrtPriceMath, Tick and TickMath and parts of the DynamicFees, Sync and PoolManager tests. They found one fuzz condition that the source does not meet, for a zero amount at a 100 percent fee (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:129 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-320), and one boundary where test and source differ (test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:143 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:328). A test whose expected value or revert the source cannot produce marks a place where the source departs from what its own tests describe. The check uses only files in this repository and compares nothing with another copy.

leads.question: Which functions of the B20 token precompile, the B20 factory 0xB20f000000000000000000000000000000000000 and the Policy Registry 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000002 can an account with no role call, and can any of them change balanceOf of another holder, make a transfer to or from the PoolManager return true while the tokens are held or sent elsewhere, or change the PoolManager's membership in a policy that a pooled token references?
leads.why: The cycle read the issuer roles of B20 and did not list what an ordinary account can do. The PoolManager holds about 5.34 million OUSD, and settle credits any rise of balanceOf since sync to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). Currency.transfer accepts any call that returns true (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). On Tempo a transfer that the recipient's receive policy rejects returns true and parks the tokens in a guard contract, which is a confirmed medium finding there. A similar rule in B20, or a balance component that a third party can add and later remove, would give a credit that is not backed or a payout that does not arrive. The B20 rules also changed at the Cobalt and Denim forks, so the documentation of the current fork must be used.

leads.question: Which tokens make up the twenty largest balances of the Arbitrum One PoolManager 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32, and for each one: who can freeze, seize, pause or upgrade it, does USDT0 there carry destroyBlockedFunds, and does any function that an ordinary account can call change balanceOf(PoolManager) without a transfer (rebase, reward claim for a holder, reflection)?
leads.why: The issuer control finding is confirmed on eleven chains and nobody checked Arbitrum One. The second half of the question looks for the unprivileged case: a balance rise between sync and settle is credited to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and a balance drop without a take leaves pools short (assumption A2).

leads.question: For the twenty largest token balances of the PoolManager on Polygon and on Avalanche, who holds freeze, seize, pause and upgrade roles, and can an ordinary account change balanceOf(PoolManager) of any of them without a transfer? Should the cleared item on Circle USDC for these two chains become part of the issuer finding?
leads.why: The unit recorded the USDC blocklist on these chains as cleared while five other units rate the same hazard high, and it listed no other pooled asset. The rebasing stETH finding on Ethereum shows that balances which move without transfers do sit in the PoolManager. PoS bridged tokens on Polygon and bridged tokens on Avalanche have their own mint and upgrade paths.

leads.question: Which tokens does the PoolManager hold on OP Mainnet, Zora and World Chain beyond the main stablecoins, and does any of them have issuer controls or a balance that an ordinary account can change without a transfer?
leads.why: The three profiles repeat the generic OP Stack text for this lens, and Zora has no delta of high relevance at all. The stablecoin finding of this unit covers six chains and leaves Zora out without saying why.

leads.question: Does USDG on Ink (0xe343167631d89B6Ffc58B88d6b7fB0228795491D, about 767,000 held by the PoolManager) use the claimable rewards design that the verifier found in USDG on Robinhood Chain, is the PoolManager registered in a payout group or named as a claim destination, and who can trigger a claim?
leads.why: On Robinhood Chain balanceOf excludes unclaimed rewards and a claim moves tokens from a claim source to a destination without a call by the destination. A claim that credits the PoolManager between a caller's sync and settle is booked to that caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). If any account can trigger such a claim, rewards meant for the PoolManager's balance can be taken by whoever times the call. The op-stack-eth verifier could not find where the freeze logic of USDG on Ink lives, so the implementation there is unread.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain on 2026-12-08, does any CAS20 token or reserved address expose the native BNB balance of an account through balanceOf and transfer? On Base, does any B20 token, precompile or planned Base Transactions fee token expose native ETH in the same way?
leads.why: A second face of the native asset is confirmed on Celo, Arc, Polygon, OP Mainnet and Zora, and the code handles it only because settle rejects msg.value while a token is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356). Each new face is a new currency id that shares the native balance, and its transfer and balanceOf rules decide whether the two ledgers stay jointly covered. Both chains are adding token logic that runs in the node, and nobody asked this question for them.

leads.question: On Elysium, which contracts on HyperEVM hold the rollup's inbox, bridge escrow and assertion logic, does a delayed inbox message and a forced inclusion call fit into a 3,000,000 gas HyperEVM block, and can HyperCore system transactions move tokens held by the bridge escrow?
leads.why: Elysium settles to HyperEVM. Every hazard recorded for HyperEVM (small blocks, system transactions that move token balances, the bridge to HyperCore) applies to the parent chain contracts that back all bridged assets in Elysium pools and to the only exit that does not depend on the single sequencer. The unit treated Elysium as stock Nitro and did not look at the parent chain.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the system contracts of BNB Smart Chain (0x1000 to 0x1008, 0x2000 to 0x2006, 0x3000), of Polygon (0x1000, 0x1001) and every precompile address in the Avalanche C-Chain client source return for transfer(address,uint256) with zero and nonzero amount, balanceOf(PoolManager), each IHooks selector and empty calldata with zero value?
leads.why: take makes the PoolManager call transfer on any address the caller names, sync makes it call balanceOf, and initialize makes it call hook selectors (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). The sweep was done on Ethereum, the Arbitrum chains, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc and HyperEVM. On these three chains only 0x1010 on Polygon was tested and the Avalanche list came from documentation. A target that returns true or empty data to transfer, or a changing number to balanceOf, needs a follow up.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the predeploys 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000000 to 0x42000000000000000000000000000000000000ff, the Base registries 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000001 and 0x8453000000000000000000000000000000000002 and the World Chain PBH contracts return for transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(PoolManager) and empty calldata with zero value, and what does a native take with value to L2ToL1MessagePasser 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000016 do?
leads.why: The unit tested predeploys as hook addresses and tested WETH and LegacyERC20ETH as currencies. The full sweep with the currency call shapes is not recorded. The message passer has a receive function that calls initiateWithdrawal(msg.sender, 100000, empty data) (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/develop/packages/contracts-bedrock/src/L2/L2ToL1MessagePasser.sol, lines 60 to 62), and an eth_call with from set to the PoolManager, value 1 wei and empty calldata succeeds on OP Mainnet and Base. A native take to it would send the amount to the PoolManager's own address on L1, which is the same pattern as the confirmed HyperEVM finding on payouts to the HyperCore bridge address. The caller is debited the amount (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the expected result is a loss for the caller only, and that should be confirmed.

leads.question: With from set to the PoolManager address, what do the OP Stack predeploys on Celo and X Layer, the Celo core contracts LockedGold and FeeHandler, the transfer precompile at 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000fd and the X Layer gasless whitelist contract return for transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(PoolManager), each IHooks selector and empty calldata with zero value?
leads.why: Same sweep as on the other chains. On Celo the CELO token and the fee currencies were tested, and the critic tested the four fee currency adapters, which answer balanceOf and revert on transfer. The other system contracts on both chains have no recorded test. Celo's native asset can be moved by contract calls through a precompile, so a second caller path into that precompile would matter for every native pool (assumption A3).

leads.question: Do the Karst bundle or any fork bundle scheduled for Celo and X Layer contain upgrade deposits sent from the zero address, and does failedMessages of the L2CrossDomainMessenger on either chain hold a message from the Ethereum timelock that anyone could replay?
leads.why: protocolFeeController is the zero address on both chains. Two verifiers rejected the clearance of the zero sender on the other OP Stack chains because the Ecotone and Isthmus bundles used zero address senders, and the clearance for Celo and X Layer did not consider this. The replay question transfers the Polygon lead on failed state syncs: a stale governance message that failed on first delivery could restore an old controller. The reach in both cases is the protocol fee (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-57).

leads.question: Do the X Layer release notes, node configuration published by OKX or operator statements show the risk control filter enabled on the mainnet sequencer, and is there a valid transaction to 0x360e68faccca8ca495c1b759fd9eee466db9fb32 or to a pooled token that was visible to other nodes and stayed unincluded?
leads.why: This one fact settles the plausible finding on the X Layer filter. If the filter is off, the finding is a dormant capability and stays low. If it is on with a rule that can match the PoolManager, the verdict says medium applies.

leads.question: Has any transaction that touches a contract on the Soneium restriction list been included after it was submitted through an RPC endpoint not run by the operator?
leads.why: The Soneium finding is confirmed with secondary evidence for blocking at the sequencer. The primary source describes blocking at the RPC only. One included transaction shows the block is at the RPC, and then any other endpoint is enough and the L1 route is not needed.

leads.question: On Tempo and Arc, does any protocol rule read an account's token or native balance during a transaction and grant something that lasts beyond it (fee sponsorship, payment lane access, validator or channel deposits, storage credits), so that tokens taken from the PoolManager for the length of one unlock have value?
leads.why: take hands out any pooled balance before payment, and the only condition is that deltas net to zero when unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-297). Assumption A5 was tested on Ethereum, Celo and HyperEVM. The two chains whose protocol is built around stablecoin balances were not asked.

leads.question: What does it cost in each currency to fill the lowest and the highest usable tick of a pool to tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick for tick spacings 1, 60 and 200, and is there a deployed hook or vault that must add a position on those ticks inside its withdrawal path, so that a full tick blocks an exit?
leads.why: The accounting unit computed about 1.9e12 base units at spacing 60 and filed the result under cleared because removals are never gated by the cap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:165-173). Blocking deposits alone is griefing. It becomes a freeze only for a contract that has to add liquidity on a full tick before it can pay out. The numbers were not checked by the verifier.
